name: Nikhil Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at a big bauxite mine. My job is keeping the haul roads smooth, so the hundred-tonne trucks don't wreck their tyres and nobody slides off a bend in the wet. I'm about a year and a half in, and before that I ran a phone repair shop in town for eleven years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why the switch from phones to a grader?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The shop was fine but flat, and with two kids and a mortgage I wanted steadier money. I kept the repair side going as an online thing, refurbished phones, mostly evenings. On the grader I'm still learning to cut a proper crossfall, the slope that lets water run off, and my supervisor Hamid says I overthink it. I probably do. I ask an AI app about road drainage on my lunch break, which he finds very funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Sounds a bit boring, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. I'd still say the tools are useful, because they are, for me. I'd probably post something like, still handy, just not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a tiny bit disappointed. I like the idea of what's possible. But for the family, it's simple: I keep my job, I keep the side business, we're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep grading roads and get my loader ticket next year so I'm more useful. I'd keep using AI to write my phone listings and answer customer messages, which saves me a couple of hours a week. And we'd keep the savings ticking along, about three months now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI saves you time on the phone business. How exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It writes the listings from my notes, checks the model numbers and drafts replies when someone asks if a phone's unlocked. I still check everything. It turns a two-hour Sunday job into forty minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner think about you using AI so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina thinks I'm a bit obsessed. She works at a dental clinic and they brought in AI for booking, and she says it's annoying half the time. We argue about it in a friendly way.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold, but the tools are still useful for me. I'd post something like 'still handy, just not magic'.
S0.think: I'd be a tiny bit disappointed, because I like what's possible. For the family it's simple: I keep my job and the side business, and we're fine.
S0.do: Keeps grading roads and gets a loader ticket next year. Keeps using AI to write phone listings and answer customers, and keeps about three months of savings growing.
S0.quote: It turns a two-hour Sunday job into forty minutes.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil already uses AI to run his evening phone business, so a plateau changes little for him. He's mildly disappointed rather than relieved. His partner's scepticism gives a friendly counterweight at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right for where things are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, if you're willing to learn. Some jobs will go, that's true, but the people who pick up the new tools early will do okay. I'd say that at work, though I'd say it gently, because some of the guys would hate hearing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a decent spot. Graders are one of the machines they're automating now, with GPS guidance, and I know phones and software better than most on site. I'd want to be the guy who sets them up and fixes them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Hamid this month about the GPS grade control system they're trialling and put my hand up to learn it. I'd do the online courses from the machine maker in the evenings. I'd also start selling repaired tablets alongside phones, because I've got the tools already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Interested, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some guys would hate hearing it. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Col, who's been grading for thirty years. He can feel a road through the seat. He'd say a computer can't do that, and he'd be partly right, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo's fourteen and loves coding, so I'd tell him to keep at it but also learn something with his hands. Ruby's nine, she'd just want to know if I'm still taking her to swimming.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance if you're willing to learn, and the people who pick up new tools early will do okay. I'd say it gently, because some colleagues would hate hearing it.
S1.think: I think I'm in a decent spot, because graders are already being automated with GPS guidance and I know software better than most on site. I want to be the one who sets them up and fixes them.
S1.do: Asks his supervisor this month to join the GPS grade control trial and takes the machine maker's online courses in the evenings. Expands his side business to repaired tablets.
S1.quote: He can feel a road through the seat.
S1.fieldNote: Nikhil turns steady disruption into a role he wants: the person who sets up and fixes the automated graders. He respects the older operator's skill even while he expects machines to take it over. He's careful about how his optimism lands with colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to figure out fast how people get paid when machines do the work. I'm not a big politics person, but I'd back whatever works, a basic income, a tax on robots, I don't mind which. You can't have a town full of people with nothing to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. My plan was to be the guy who fixes the machines, but if AGI fixes them too, there's no guy. The phone business would shrink too, because people would just get a robot to repair them or buy new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd learn whatever the new systems are, because the last people standing will be the ones who understand them. I'd put some savings into shares in the companies making the robots, a small amount, because if they're taking the jobs I want a slice. We'd cut back on eating out and the trip to see Lina's parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited about the technology and scared about the paycheque, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too short to build something new that the machines can't do. With five or ten I'd find a gap. With two, I'm just running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy shares. With a mortgage and three months saved, is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and Lina would say so too. I'd keep it small, maybe two thousand. It's a hedge, not a plan.

S2.say: I'd say we need to work out fast how people get paid when machines do the work. I'd back whatever works, a basic income or a robot tax.
S2.think: I think my plan to fix the machines falls apart if AGI fixes them too. The phone business would shrink as well.
S2.do: Learns the new systems in the first months to be among the last needed. Puts about two thousand into shares in robot makers as a hedge, and cuts eating out and a family trip.
S2.feel: Anxious, excited about the technology and scared about the paycheque at the same time.
S2.quote: If they're taking the jobs I want a slice.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI is the first picture that breaks Nikhil's plan, and he says so plainly. His response is still to learn and to place a small bet on the robot makers. He holds mixed feelings openly: excitement and fear together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. Get the kids learning practical and tech skills, get adults into courses. I'd post some of the free courses I've found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is enough for me to move once, maybe into setting up and checking automated machines across a few mines. That buys time and money. It doesn't make me safe at the end, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the grade control course in the first year and ask to move into the technical team. I'd grow the phone business a bit, maybe a stall at the Saturday market, so there's more than one income. And I'd lift savings to five months before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a point where you'd stop chasing the next skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably when the kids are through school. Leo would be nineteen by then. After that, if the money's sorted, I'd ease off and take whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hamid say about you moving to the technical team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh and say finally, someone to fix the screen in my cab. He'd back me, he's that kind of supervisor.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now, with kids learning practical and tech skills and adults in courses. I'd share free courses online.
S3.think: I think five years lets me move once, maybe into setting up automated machines across several mines. It buys time and money, not safety at the end.
S3.do: Takes the grade control course in the first year and moves into the technical team. Grows the phone business with a Saturday market stall and lifts savings to five months before 2031.
S3.quote: It doesn't make me safe at the end, though.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Nikhil a clear middle step and a second income. He's honest that it's a bridge, not a solution. His milestone is his son finishing school, after which he'd ease off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's enough to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so let's get going. Learn the tools, plan the money, help the people who find it hard. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown, I'd have moved into the technical side and maybe built the phone business into a proper shop again. And by then it'd be everyone's problem, not just mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into the technical team over the first couple of years and keep learning. I'd use AI to automate more of the phone business, the stock and the listings, so it runs with less of my time. And I'd put a little into shares each month, nothing crazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Curious about what it'll look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it'd be everyone's problem by then. Is that comforting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strangely, yes. If the whole world's dealing with it, there'll be some system. It's being the only one caught out that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the mine to do with that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Train the operators to run the new gear, don't just hire new people for it. We already know the roads, the weather, the trucks.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long runway: learn the tools, plan the money, and help people who find it hard.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine at fifty-three with the kids grown, a technical role and maybe a proper phone shop again. By then it'd be everyone's problem, not just mine.
S4.do: Moves into the technical team over the first couple of years and keeps learning. Uses AI to automate stock and listings in the phone business, and puts a little into shares each month.
S4.quote: It's being the only one caught out that scares me.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Nikhil's adaptability and side business carry him to calm. He finds comfort in a shared problem rather than a personal one. He wants the mine to retrain its own operators.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. What would help is a clear plan for how people get paid when work dries up, whatever it's called. And training that's free and short, so you can try things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the grader, weirdly. There's something about cutting a perfect road at dawn that a phone screen never gave me.

headlineQuote: There's something about cutting a perfect road at dawn that a phone screen never gave me.
portrait: Nikhil Zhang is 43, drives a grader on the haul roads at a bauxite mine and ran a phone repair shop for eleven years before that. He's pragmatic, uses AI every day and runs a refurbished phone business in the evenings. He sees Steady Disruption as his chance to become the person who sets up automated graders, but fast AGI breaks that plan and makes him anxious. With five or ten years he builds a technical role and a second income, and takes comfort that it would be everyone's problem.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there'd be no time to build anything the machines can't do.
whatWouldHelp: A clear plan for how people get paid when work dries up, and free, short training so people can try new things.
